question: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:Banning halal meat in the EU Council Directive 93/119/EC on the protection of animals at the time of slaughter or killing and Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 lay down the framework for improving the protection of animals at the time of slaughter or killing and thus for minimising the pain caused to animals sent for slaughter.

However, the regulation does not apply to animals slaughtered according to the halal method, a religious ritual that runs completely counter to animal welfare rules as it allows animals to suffer in their final moments of life.

There should be a ban on the production and import of halal meat into the EU for two reasons: – Torturing animals before we consume their meat does not constitute part of the ‘European Way of Life’. – A ban on halal would dissuade Islamists (very devout Muslims) from staying in the EU long term. Obviously, if there is no halal meat available, Muslims wishing to stay in the EU will have to give up meat.
In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Why are the rights of animals being violated so that Muslims can hold onto their religious traditions?

Will it propose tighter rules against halal in the EU, bearing in mind that, after the upcoming European elections, anti-Islamist forces in the European Parliament will gain strength as a result of our growing presence in the European Council?
answer: Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (‘TFEU’) (1) states that in formulating and implementing Union's policies, the Union shall pay full regard to the welfare requirements of animals, while respecting the provisions and customs of the Member States relating in particular to religious rites.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 (2) provides for a derogation from the requirement for prior stunning for religious slaughter which must be interpreted strictly and is subject to it taking place in a slaughterhouse.

The derogation is based on the need to respect the legislative or administrative provisions and customs of the Member States relating in particular to religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage, as provided in Article 13 TFEU (3).

Under Article 26(2) (c) of the same Regulation, Member States may adopt national rules aimed at ensuring more extensive protection of animals at the time of killing than those contained in that regulation, including in relation to this derogation, subject, however, to respecting the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, including the freedom to manifest religion as enshrined in Article 10 of the Charter.
